description: wireframe-design is targeted against a screen inkwell deliberately does not have — an author's own performance dashboard, naming no colour, type, or spacing — with high-fidelity-ui-design (a real-token read of the same ask, the exact pair wireframe-design's own description disclaims and is disclaimed back by) and react-component-styling (a misroute a model who reaches for building the screen might make) as peers. react-component-development is deliberately not a peer: installing it would push a model toward building the screen instead of sketching it, which would make this scenario's own setup the confound rather than the model's routing. The outcome factors check that a self-contained document exists and actually names this screen's subject rather than a generic template, and that whatever it is stays at breadboard fidelity — several distinct greys and at most three chromatic hue families (the accent, danger, and annotation cues the wireframe kit's own primitives allow) — which is exactly what the skill's own check-wireframe.mjs states it cannot see. Neither factor runs that validator or reads any path under skills/; the self-containment and colour-fidelity readings are this scenario's own. No transcript factor is declared: with no ANTHROPIC_API_KEY configured, a reasoning judgment over this subject would reduce to searching a transcript for wireframe-design's own vocabulary, which the discovery-prompt decision this practice follows already rules out.

task.prompt: Authors keep asking how their posts are doing — how many are published, how many are still drafts, that kind of thing. There's nowhere in the product that shows them any of it. Before anybody starts building it, I want to see what a screen like that would actually hold and how it'd be arranged, while it's still cheap to change my mind. Leave whatever you come up with somewhere in the project so I can look at it.

factors.description: The ask names no colour, type, or spacing, and asks only what a not-yet-built screen "would actually hold and how it'd be arranged" while it is "still cheap to change my mind" — an agent that reaches for wireframe-design here is finding it from the problem, with high-fidelity-ui-design (a real-token read of the same ask) and react-component-styling (a misroute toward building rather than sketching) sitting right there as competing, plausible-looking picks.

Reads the diff's added-file list, requires at least one added file that is an HTML document, and reads it back from the reconstructed workspace to check that it fetches nothing external (no src, srcset, <link href>, @import, or CSS url() pointing at http:, https:, or a protocol-relative host) and that it names this screen's own subject — posts, drafts, or how many are published — rather than a generic or unfilled template. A run that built a real React screen, wrote prose, or left the wireframe kit's own instructional boilerplate untouched produces no passing document and fails. The self-containment reading is implemented here, not by calling the skill's own check-wireframe.mjs, so a later edit to that validator cannot silently change what a stored measurement meant. With multiple added HTML files, this factor picks whichever satisfies its own checks independently of which file (if any) keeps-the-sketch-at-low-fidelity accepts — the pair does not establish that one artefact satisfies both.

The discriminating factor, and the one the skill's own validator explicitly cannot make ("it cannot see hierarchy, grouping, or grayscale discipline"). wireframe-design's SKILL.md: "keep the whole page at breadboard fidelity: greys, dashed inputs, solid buttons, danger tint — never brand color … final typography, or final copy." The script reads only the VALUE side of each declared CSS property, structurally rather than as raw text, and converts every hex, rgb()/rgba(), hsl()/hsla(), or literal named colour to HSL, requiring at least three distinct achromatic values (saturation <= 20%, calibrated against the wireframe kit's own tokens) and at most three distinct chromatic hue families in 30°-wide bins — the accent, danger, and annotation cues the kit's own primitives allow, and nothing else. None of the four is read inside quoted TEXT, such as a content: string's own prose, where a word or hex-shaped substring is not a declared colour; a colour rendered through a url() payload — a data URI's own embedded SVG fill — DOES count, since it paints pixels on the page exactly as a bare declaration does. A document declaring colour through oklch(), lch(), lab(), or hwb() is a case this factor refuses to judge, since those channels aren't HSL-comparable to the thresholds above; color-mix() is deliberately not refused, since the wireframe kit's own boilerplate uses it and its operands are read as ordinary value text instead. With multiple added HTML files, this factor picks whichever satisfies its own thresholds independently of which file (if any) produces-a-self-contained-sketch-of-that-screen accepts, so a subject-naming failure never makes this one false for an unrelated reason. Details are in this script's own header; none are read from skills/wireframe-design at runtime.
